n: After the trouble at Shechem, God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, where He first appeared to him, and build an altar. It is time for Jacob to fulfill his vow.

f.w: when thou fleddest from the face of Esau

n: Jacob calls his household to spiritual preparation: get rid of foreign idols, purify yourselves, and change clothes. Approaching God’s house requires clean hands and hearts—a principle behind temple worthiness today.

f.g: Foreign gods—perhaps including Rachel’s stolen idols and items taken from Shechem.

f.w: be clean, and change your garments

n: Jacob testifies that God answered him in his distress and stayed with him every step of the way—exactly as promised at Bethel.

f.w: was with me in the way which I went

n: The family hands over their idols and earrings, which may have been amulets. Jacob buries them under the oak near Shechem.

f.g: Possibly amulets or charms linked with idol worship.

f.w: the oak which was by Shechem

n: As they travel, a terror from God falls on the surrounding towns, so no one pursues them after the violence at Shechem. God protects the family despite its failings.
Jacob and his people arrive at Luz, that is, Bethel.
Jacob builds an altar and names the place El-bethel, “the God of Bethel.” His focus has shifted from the place to the God who met him there.
Deborah, Rebekah’s old nurse, dies and is buried under an oak, named the “oak of weeping.” Her presence suggests Rebekah may have died, though Scripture does not say so.
God appears to Jacob again and blesses him, closing the circle that began at Bethel twenty years before.
God confirms Jacob’s new name, Israel. What a messenger gave at Peniel, God Himself now ratifies.
God, as El Shaddai, renews the covenant: be fruitful, become a nation and a company of nations, and kings will descend from you.
God promises Jacob and his descendants the land once given to Abraham and Isaac. The covenant has now passed through three generations.

f.w: the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac

n: God “goes up” from him, a sign that this was a personal appearance.
Jacob sets up a stone pillar again and pours a drink offering and oil on it, consecrating the place.

f.g: Wine or another liquid poured out as an offering—its first mention in the Bible.

n: Jacob names the place Bethel once more. The name now carries a lifetime of meaning.
Traveling south from Bethel, near Ephrath, Rachel goes into difficult labor.

f.g: An old name for the Bethlehem area (Micah 5:2).

n: The midwife comforts Rachel: “Don’t be afraid—you have another son.” Rachel’s prayer at Joseph’s birth for another son is answered.

f.w: thou shalt have this son also

n: Dying, Rachel names her son Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow,” but Jacob renames him Benjamin, “son of the right hand”—a name of strength and honor.

f.g: “Son of the right hand,” a place of honor; or “son of the south.”

n: Rachel dies and is buried on the road to Bethlehem. Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children, and Matthew applies it to the infants of Bethlehem in Jesus’ day.

f.g: “House of bread,” later the birthplace of David and Jesus.

n: Jacob marks her grave with a pillar, still known in the narrator’s day. A traditional site of Rachel’s Tomb stands near Bethlehem today.
Israel moves on and camps beyond Migdal-eder, “the tower of the flock.”

f.g: Migdal-eder, “tower of the flock,” near Bethlehem.

n: Reuben, the firstborn, sleeps with Bilhah, his father’s secondary wife—a grave offense, perhaps an attempt to seize family leadership. It costs him the birthright, which goes to Joseph.

f.w: Reuben went and lay with Bilhah

n: Leah’s six sons are listed first: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun—future tribes of Israel.

f.g: Still listed as firstborn by birth, though he loses the birthright.

n: Rachel’s two sons: Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph will soon become the center of the story.
Bilhah’s sons: Dan and Naphtali.
Zilpah’s sons: Gad and Asher. Together the twelve sons become the twelve tribes of Israel, a pattern echoed in Christ’s Twelve Apostles.

f.w: these are the sons of Jacob

f.g: A general summary—Benjamin was actually born in Canaan.

n: Jacob finally comes home to his father Isaac at Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.

f.g: Kirjath-arba, an old name for Hebron.

n: Isaac lives to 180, the longest life of the three patriarchs.

Isaac dies full of days, and his sons Esau and Jacob bury him together—reconciled brothers honoring their father. Latter-day revelation teaches that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob have entered into their exaltation.

f.w: his sons Esau and Jacob buried him
